title: LLM Architecture & Scaling
summary: The decoder-only architecture behind GPT-style models, and how scale predictably changes what they can do.

slides.markdown:
A **large language model** is a decoder-only Transformer trained to predict the next token, over and over, on a huge slice of the internet. Everything an LLM does — chat, code, reasoning — is that one skill at scale.

Think of it as a well-read autocomplete: it never "decides" to answer, it keeps predicting the most plausible next token given everything so far, including your prompt.

- **Architecture:** decoder-only, autoregressive, left to right.
- **Training:** next-token prediction on trillions of tokens.
- **Scale:** capability grows predictably, then sometimes jumps.

slides.subTitle: Decoder-only, GPT-style
slides.markdown:
GPT-style LLMs use only the **decoder** half of the original Transformer ([Attention & Transformer Architecture](attention-transformer-architecture) has the full mechanics). Each token can only attend to itself and the tokens **before** it — a causal mask blocks any peek at the future.

That asymmetry is the whole point: at generation time you only have the past, so training must match. Stack dozens of these masked self-attention + feedforward blocks and you get a model that turns "everything so far" into a probability distribution over the next token.

slides.subTitle: Pretraining: predict the next token
slides.markdown:
The pretraining objective is almost embarrassingly simple: given a chunk of text, predict the next token, compute the cross-entropy loss against the actual next token, and back-propagate. No labels beyond the text itself — the text **is** the label, shifted by one position.

Repeated across trillions of tokens, this single objective is enough to force the model to internalize grammar, facts, style, and rough reasoning patterns, because all of them help predict the next token better somewhere in the corpus.

slides.subTitle: Byte-pair encoding and vocabulary design
slides.markdown:
LLMs don't see characters or whole words — they see **tokens** from a fixed vocabulary (commonly 50k–100k+ entries) built by **byte-pair encoding (BPE)**: start from individual bytes/characters and greedily merge the most frequent adjacent pairs until the vocabulary is full.

Common words become one token; rare words split into subword pieces (`"unhappiness"` → `un`, `happi`, `ness`). This keeps the vocabulary small, handles any input without an `<unk>` token, and directly sets your **context budget** — a bigger vocabulary means more tokens per model call cost the same words fewer tokens.

slides.subTitle: Loss improves predictably with scale
slides.markdown:
**Scaling laws** are the empirical finding that test loss falls in a smooth, predictable power-law curve as you increase **model parameters**, **training data**, and **compute** together — not haphazardly, but along a curve you can fit and extrapolate before training the largest run.

The practical upshot (Chinchilla-style results): for a fixed compute budget, there's an optimal ratio of parameters to training tokens — many earlier large models were actually **under-trained** relative to their size, and a smaller model trained on more data can beat a bigger, data-starved one.

slides.subTitle: Context window and KV caching
slides.markdown:
The **context window** is the max tokens (prompt + generated so far) the model attends over at once. Self-attention cost grows **quadratically** with sequence length, so doubling the context roughly quadruples the attention compute.

**KV caching** makes generation practical anyway: once a token's key/value vectors are computed, they're cached and reused each later step instead of recomputed. Without it, token 1,000 would redo the math for all 999 prior tokens; with it, each new token only computes its own. A bigger cache is still why long-context requests cost more and run slower.

slides.subTitle: Emergent abilities
slides.markdown:
Most capabilities improve **smoothly** with scale, but a few — multi-step arithmetic, some chain-of-thought reasoning, in-context learning from a handful of examples — look flat and near-random at small scale, then jump sharply past a size threshold. These are **emergent abilities**.

Why it matters: you can't always predict a new capability by extrapolating a smaller model's curve — some skills aren't there yet at 1B parameters and appear at 70B. (Some argue this is partly a measurement artifact, not true emergence — unsettled, but the planning implication holds either way.)

slides.subTitle: Bigger isn't automatically better
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The biggest available model is always the right choice."

**Why it's wrong:** scale buys general capability, not a guarantee of winning on *your* task — a small, well-tuned or prompted model can match a frontier model on a narrow job at a fraction of the cost. Scale also doesn't fix hallucination or stale knowledge; those need retrieval, tools, or verification, not more parameters.

**Correct model:** pick the smallest model that clears your quality bar, and reserve the largest models for genuinely open-ended reasoning.
